reason: The narrative does not present a contrast between regular people being wrong and leaders being right. The story opens with all of Israel collectively doing evil in God's sight (וַיֹּסִפוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת הָרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה), establishing a collective failure rather than distinguishing between people and leaders. The narrative is primarily focused on Samson as an individual deliverer empowered by God's spirit, not on a conflict between regular people and established leadership. When the men of Judah appear, they negotiate pragmatically with Samson rather than represent a leadership position that is vindicated as 'right.' The moral arc centers on Israel's sin, divine punishment, and God raising up a judge—not on validating leadership against a misguided populace.
